passage: Payal stood in the university gallery in front of a large grey canvas with a single small red mark in the corner. Her friend Vandana leaned in. "He must have been so sad when he painted this." Payal wasn't sure. "Maybe. Or maybe he's just interested in empty space. The note says he studied in a school where painters used a lot of grey." She read the label twice. "The red could mean anything: anger, a sunset, a lipstick smudge." Vandana laughed. "So we can't tell?" Payal shook her head. "We can say what it makes us feel. I'd just be careful saying what he felt."

qa.q: What was in the corner of the grey canvas?
qa.a: There was a single small red mark in the corner.

qa.q: What might Vandana be thinking about the painter, and why does Payal disagree?
qa.a: Vandana assumed he was very sad, while Payal said he might just be interested in empty space, so the mood is not certain.

qa.q: What could Vandana do to learn more before judging the painter's mood?
qa.a: Vandana could read the gallery note, learn about the school of painting, and treat her guess as one view.

qa.q: How might the painter feel about being told his painting shows sadness?
qa.a: He might be amused or disagree if he was thinking about form and tradition, so the viewer's reading and his intent can differ.

grounding: Payal interprets a painting with humility, separating her reaction from the artist's actual mood.

"This film is so dark," Aditi said as the credits rolled in the dorm lounge. "The director must be depressed."
"Maybe," Zainab said, tucking her feet under her. "Or he might just love that style."
"But every scene is at night."
"That's a choice. It can be a craft thing or a story thing. It doesn't have to say how he feels in his own life."
Aditi frowned. "So I can't say anything?"
"You can say what it did to you. It made you feel low, right?"
"It did. I felt like I'd been left in a cold room."
"That's a good thing to know. Just don't diagnose the man."

qa.q: When are the scenes in the film set?
qa.a: Every scene is at night.

qa.q: What does Aditi feel about the film, and what did Aditi assume about the director?
qa.a: Aditi felt low, like she'd been left in a cold room, and Aditi assumed, without evidence, that the director must be depressed.

qa.q: What could Aditi do to talk about the film without guessing the director's state?
qa.a: Aditi could describe what the film did to them and what choices she noticed, like the night scenes.

qa.q: How might the director see Aditi's guess about his mood?
qa.a: He might find it odd, since darkness in a film can come from style or story rather than his own feelings.

grounding: Aditi and Zainab discuss a film and learn that a maker's mood cannot be safely inferred from the work.

passage: At the college gallery's student show, Payal and I stood in front of a huge dark canvas: black, deep blue, one thin red line. I'm Ayesha. I said confidently, "Whoever painted this was really depressed." Payal raised her eyebrows. "Maybe." That evening the painter, a third-year named Rizwan, gave a short talk. He said he'd been studying an old Japanese ink style that uses mostly dark tones, and the red line was a trick he'd learned to lead the eye. He said he'd painted it during the happiest month of his year, after his sister's wedding. I felt silly. I'd read his whole mind from the colours. Payal whispered, "You'd have said the same about half the paintings in the museum." Since then, when I look at art, I try to say, "This makes me feel…", not "the artist felt…".

qa.q: What was the painting's one bright element?
qa.a: One thin red line.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel after hearing Rizwan's talk?
qa.a: Ayesha felt silly and a bit embarrassed for assuming the painter was depressed from the colours.

qa.q: What habit did Ayesha adopt, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Saying "This makes me feel…" instead of "the artist felt…", because a maker's mood can't be safely read from the work alone.

qa.q: How did Rizwan explain the dark painting?
qa.a: He said it came from studying an old ink style and a technique to lead the eye, and he painted it during a happy month.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that art reflects craft and tradition, so the maker's mood can't be inferred from the work alone.

passage:
Film studies teacher's note, Tuesday seminar.
Today we watched a short black-and-white film about an old man feeding pigeons. Anjali, in the discussion, said firmly, "The director must be lonely. You can feel it." Several students nodded. I asked Darshan, who had read the director's interview for homework, to share what he'd found. The director had made the film as a comedy about his own father, who is surrounded by family and loves pigeons, and chose black and white because of a festival rule. Anjali looked embarrassed, then curious. She asked, "So the loneliness is just in me?" I said her reading was valid as her own response, but that we can't safely read the director's mood from the screen. Craft, tradition and audience all shape a film. I've asked the class to write two paragraphs next week: one on what the film made them feel, one on what they know of how it was made.
— Mr Kurian

qa.q: Why did the director choose black and white?
qa.a: Because of a festival rule.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel when she heard about the director's interview?
qa.a: She looked embarrassed, then curious, wondering if the loneliness she felt came from her.

qa.q: What did Mr Kurian do that helped the class read films more carefully?
qa.a: He validated Anjali's feeling as her own response, explained the limits of inferring the director's mood, and set a task separating feeling from facts.

qa.q: What had Darshan found in the director's interview?
qa.a: That the film was a comedy about the director's own father, who is surrounded by family and loves pigeons.

grounding: Shows a young adult forming a view of a filmmaker's mood and learning that craft and context mean the maker's state can't be inferred from the work.

passage:
Thursday night.
Went to the screening of Kashish's friend's short film at the film club. The film was so bleak: rain, an empty bus stop, a girl waiting for someone who never came. I left thinking the director must be heartbroken. I even asked Kashish, very seriously, if her friend was okay.
Kashish laughed so hard. "Tara? She's the most cheerful person I know. She made it for an assignment on 'waiting'. The rain was a sprinkler, and she had to reshoot because she kept giggling."
I felt a bit foolish. I'd built a whole sad story about a person from twelve minutes of film.
But the film did make me feel something real. That part's mine, I think. The director's feelings are hers, and I don't know them.
— Bhupen

qa.q: What was Tara's film made for?
qa.a: An assignment on 'waiting'.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel after Kashish's explanation?
qa.a: Bhupen felt a bit foolish for building a whole sad story about the director from the film.

qa.q: What distinction does Bhupen draw at the end?
qa.a: That the feeling the film gave Bhupen is real and Bhupen's own, but the director's feelings can't be known from the film.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Tara?
qa.a: As the most cheerful person she knows, who kept giggling during the shoot of a bleak film.

grounding: Shows a young adult assuming a filmmaker's mood from a bleak film and learning the maker's state can't be inferred from the work.
